Chapter Nine: The Politics of Taste—Power, Privilege, and Whose Stories Get Told.
Taste is such a slippery thing, isn’t it? What one person calls a masterpiece, someone else might see as a complete eyesore.
Let’s wade into those murky waters and ask the big question: who actually gets to decide what counts as “good” or “important” art? And even more—what gets left out when those decisions are made?
Imagine this: a high school student, heart pounding, shares their favorite song with the class. But instead of smiles, they're met with blank stares... and a dismissive shrug from the teacher.
That moment? It stings. The student quietly learns that some tastes are valued more than others.
It’s a small scene, but it speaks volumes. It shows how taste is shaped by power—by who gets to speak, who gets to judge, and whose stories are seen as worth telling.
The story of taste stretches back centuries. Picture the exclusive salons of eighteenth-century Europe, where only a select few decided what was “refined.”
Fast forward to today, and the gatekeepers might look more like streaming platform algorithms than powdered wigs.
But the pattern’s still there—taste is never really neutral. It’s shaped by culture, by class, by race, and by gender.
Maybe you’ve noticed: a museum celebrates certain artists while ignoring others. Or a school curriculum includes some voices, but leaves the rest out.
Over time, all those choices add up. They shape what we see, what we value, and even what we believe is possible.
But here’s where things get interesting—taste isn’t set in stone. It can change, sometimes in the most unexpected places.
Picture a community theater. The people come together to stage a play that’s been ignored by the mainstream.
Sure, the production is a little rough around the edges, but the audience is truly moved. For a moment, the boundaries of “taste” get redrawn.
Suddenly, it’s clear: taste isn’t fixed. It’s fluid. Always open to challenge, to revision, to something new.
So, what can we do with this? Well, the essays invite us to question our own tastes—to really notice how much they’ve been shaped by the world around us.
Most of us, at some point, have felt the sting of being left out. Or maybe the thrill of discovering something that feels fresh and unexpected.
The politics of taste, it turns out, aren’t just about art. They’re about whose voices we hear, whose stories we tell, and whose lives we decide to value.
